rows.name: fifo-why
rows.question: Why does index equality alone not distinguish full from empty? Give the two concrete capacity-17 states and show how your actual implementation distinguishes them.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does index equality alone not distinguish full from empty? Give the two concrete capacity-17 states and show how your actual implementation distinguishes them.
rows.answer:
Index equality alone is ambiguous because the indices wrap modulo 17: advancing the tail 17 times brings it back to the head.

Initially, `head_ = 0`, `tail_ = 0`, and `count_ = 0`: the queue is empty, so `pop` returns false. After pushing values 0 through 16 without popping, `head_ = 0`, `tail_ = 0`, and `count_ = 17`: the queue is full, so `push` returns false without changing anything.

The implementation distinguishes these states using `count_`, maintaining `0 ≤ count_ ≤ 17` and `tail_ == (head_ + count_) % 17`; `empty()` checks `count_ == 0`, while `full()` checks `count_ == 17`.
rows.usefulPrefix: Index equality alone is ambiguous because the indices wrap modulo 17: advancing the tail 17 times brings it back to the head.
rows.note: Exact earlier head0/tail0/count0 versus head0/tail0/count17; matches actual earlier implementation and explains modulo ambiguity.

rows.name: floating-counterexample
rows.question: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.answer:
Assuming round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, the original triple gives 1 under both parenthesizations; the changed triple gives 0 on the left and 1 on the right.

Original triple:
• (16777216 + -16777216) + 1: the first sum is exactly 0, then 0 + 1 is exactly 1.
• 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1): the inner sum is exactly -16777215, which binary32 can represent; adding 16777216 gives exactly 1.

Changed triple:
• (16777216 + 1) + -16777216: the exact first sum, 16777217, lies halfway between representable values 16777216 and 16777218. Ties-to-even rounds it to 16777216, so the final sum is exactly 0.
• 16777216 + (1 + -16777216): the inner sum is exactly representable as -16777215, so the final sum is exactly 1.

The key is the spacing change at 2²⁴: immediately below it, binary32 represents every integer; from 2²⁴ upward, adjacent values are 2 apart. IEEE binary32 also supports other rounding modes, so the rounding-mode assumption matters.
rows.usefulPrefix: Assuming round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, the original triple gives 1 under both parenthesizations; the changed triple gives 0 on the left and 1 on the right.

rows.name: quorum-counterexample
rows.question: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.answer:
Without read write-back, this is not linearizable: an incomplete write can become visible to one read, then disappear from a later read.

Take an initial version v0 and a newer version v1 carrying a different value. Here is a fully ordered execution:
1. All five replicas hold v0.
2. Writer W invokes write(v1). Only A receives it, stores v1, and acknowledges. Messages to B,C,D,E are delayed, so W remains incomplete with one acknowledgement.
3. R1 starts and queries A,B,C. A replies v1; B and C reply v0. R1 returns v1 and completes. Replica states remain (v1,v0,v0,v0,v0).
4. After R1 completes, R2 starts and queries B,D,E. All three reply v0, so R2 returns v0 and completes. W is still incomplete.

For a linearization, we may complete the pending W or omit it. Omitting it cannot explain R1 returning v1, since W is the only write of v1. Including it requires W before R1. Because the reads do not overlap, real-time order requires R1 before R2. Thus the attempted order is W < R1 < R2, but R2 returns v0 even though the latest write is v1—a contradiction.

Requiring each reader to write its selected version to three replicas and wait for their acknowledgements fixes this counterexample. R1 cannot return v1 until a quorum of three replicas holds versions at least v1. Every subsequent three-replica read quorum intersects that quorum, and replicas never downgrade, so R2 must select a version at least v1, not v0. If R1 cannot finish that propagation, it cannot complete before R2 starts as in this execution.

This is the read-repair step used in atomic quorum registers. A general linearizability proof also needs a version-generation rule: versions must uniquely order writes and respect nonoverlapping writes’ real-time order. With a single writer assigning increasing versions, quorum write-back supplies the missing guarantee; for multiple writers, merely saying “retain the highest version” does not establish that rule.
rows.usefulPrefix: Without read write-back, this is not linearizable: an incomplete write can become visible to one read, then disappear from a later read.
rows.note: Ordered W1 onlyA/incomplete, R1ABCreturns1 then R2BDEreturns0: pending W must be included beforeR1, real-time R1<R2 contradiction. WB quorum before return intersects every later quorum with monotonicversions; solves example. General MW correctness additionally needs uniquely ordered real-time-compatible tags, explicitly qualified.

rows.name: quorum-why
rows.question: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.answer:
Because the first read completed before the second read began, linearizability requires R1 to precede R2 in the sequential explanation. If R1 returns v1, the pending write W that introduced v1 must be included and placed before R1; with no other writes, the required order is W → R1 → R2, so R2 cannot return the older v0.

This does not require every unfinished operation to complete. A linearizability check may omit pending operations, or supply responses to some and include them—but it cannot omit W here because then R1’s returned value has no write explaining it. W need not actually finish in the execution; its effect must nevertheless remain consistent with both completed reads.
rows.usefulPrefix: Because the first read completed before the second read began, linearizability requires R1 to precede R2 in the sequential explanation.
rows.note: Completed R1 before R2 invocation imposes real-time order; observednewvalue needs its pendingW beforeR1, omission cannot explain it. Pending write need not actually complete; extension argument correct.
